title: Independent ideas. Extraordinary finds.
intro: A daily selection of independent games and useful Android apps, with original F7 insights and links to their creators.

entries.name: C-Dogs SDL

price.label: Free on itch.io (name your own price)

entries.summary: C-Dogs SDL is the open-source rebuild of the 1997 DOS shooter C-Dogs: an overhead run-and-gun with up to four players in cooperative or deathmatch play. You assemble a soldier from body, head and weapon parts, then blast, slide and slash through more than a hundred community-made campaigns. The campaign format is plain data, so new levels ship as folders that the game discovers, and the same build runs on desktop platforms from one codebase.
features: Up to four players in cooperative and deathmatch modes
Customisable soldier with a large weapon selection
More than 100 user-created campaigns included
Blast, slide and slash combat viewed from directly above
Rebuilds the 1997-2001 freeware C-Dogs with its relicensed graphics and campaigns
entries.insight: Most remakes preserve a game; C-Dogs SDL preserved a level-making culture. The original author relicensed the artwork so the whole package could travel, which is why a 1997 design still accepts new campaigns from players instead of sitting in a museum.

entries.name: Hypersomnia
entries.summary: Hypersomnia is a competitive top-down shooter written in modern C++ without a games engine, built around duels and larger clan fights on user-made maps. It ships a browser client, downloadable desktop builds and a server generator, so a community can run its own matches instead of depending on the developers. An in-game editor is bundled with the download.
features: One-on-one duels and larger clan battles, written in modern C++ without a games engine
Playable in a browser as well as through Windows, Linux and macOS builds
In-game map editor shipped with the client
Public tool to host and configure your own dedicated server
Distributed on Steam and directly from the project's own site
entries.insight: Hypersomnia is a reminder that multiplayer games survive on servers, not storefronts. Because the project publishes its own builds and a server generator, the community that kept it alive can still field it years after any single distribution channel closes.

entries.name: Rizu
entries.summary: Rizu is an open-source rhythm game that treats the chart library as the point. It loads several established beatmap formats, so collections built for other games can be played without conversion, and it layers on community services: leaderboards, difficulty tables and replays. Skins can be written in Lua, and the client exposes detailed play adjustments such as asynchronous input and automatic offset correction.
features: Reads bms, ksh, mid, ojn, osu, qua and sm chart formats
Leaderboards, community difficulty tables and replay support
osu! skin compatibility plus a Lua skinning API
Asynchronous input on Windows and integrated offset auto-adjustment
Large modifier set, including an anyK-to-anyK converter
entries.insight: Rhythm games live or die by how many charts they accept. Rizu's answer is to read seven established formats instead of inventing one, which turns every existing chart archive into launch content and lets players keep the library they already built.

entries.name: Max Downforce

price.label: Free on itch.io (name your own price)

entries.summary: Max Downforce is a pseudo-3D racing game written in Lua for LÖVE that deliberately revives the Pole Position shape: you must clear each lap inside a time limit while computer-driven rivals occupy the same road. It renders at 356 x 200 and scales that buffer to a large window or full screen, which keeps the pixel texture of an 8-bit racer while fitting a wide modern display.
features: Lap-by-lap time-attack structure modelled on classic pseudo-3D racers
Field of computer-controlled opponents that block the racing line
Low 356 x 200 render resolution scaled to window or full screen
Written in Lua with the LÖVE engine, with the full source published
Windows and Linux builds distributed on itch.io
entries.insight: Foppygames kept an awkward detail on purpose. Rendering at a Commodore-64-sized resolution and scaling it up is a choice about pixel discipline, and it shows how a small team can make a retro racer feel period-correct rather than merely retro-styled.

entries.name: Synthein
entries.summary: Synthein is a LÖVE-based sandbox in which you assemble a spacecraft block by block, then fight enemies that spawn while you work. Engines, weapons, armour and utility blocks each have placement rules, and allied ships can be built to the same blueprint so a fleet follows the design logic you wrote rather than a preset loadout. Releases are published from the repository, and the packaging folder carries a Linux desktop entry and a macOS property list beside the icon.
features: Grid-based ship construction from engines, weapons, armour and utility blocks
Randomly spawning hostiles to fight with the ship you just built
Allied ships that follow the player and attack nearby enemies
Spawn menu, opened in play, for placing individual blocks
Runs on LÖVE from source, with packaged releases on GitHub
entries.insight: Ship builders usually separate the garage from the battlefield. Synthein keeps both on one screen, which makes the interesting moment the compromise: every block mounted for a fight is a block not spent on the engine that has to carry it.

entries.name: Chogan

price.label: Free, no ads and no in-app purchases

entries.summary: Chogan is a collection of fifty short, finishable games inside one Android app: board, card, puzzle and arcade sets that all run from local assets. The manifest declares the vibration permission and nothing else, not even internet access, because no part of the app reaches the network. The same codebase also runs as an installable web app and as a Telegram mini app, and the developer states that both Android sources ship the same signed APK.
features: Fifty offline games spanning board, card, puzzle and arcade formats
Android manifest declares only the vibration permission, with no internet access
No ads, in-app purchases, analytics or trackers
Menu search, pinned games, recently played and new titles rows
Long-press shortcuts on the app icon launch individual games
Browser and Telegram builds run the same game code
entries.insight: Permission lists are the most honest product documentation there is. Chogan asking for vibration alone is what makes its offline claim checkable, and it shows a game anthology being used as an argument that collections do not need a backend to work.

entries.name: Mihrab

price.label: Free, with no in-app purchases in any build

entries.summary: Mihrab is a Muslim daily companion built around prayer times that match published official timetables to the printed minute, including Diyanet, Islamiska Forbundet, Morocco, Algeria and Kemenag, with on-device calculation as a fallback. Around the clock it carries the Madinah mus-haf with recitation, a prayer journal and a fasting log. Settings, saved places and journals stay on the device, encrypted at rest, and the developer states there are no accounts, ads, trackers or Google Play Services in the F-Droid build.
features: Prayer times aligned to published national and community timetables, with a month view up to a year ahead
Falls back to on-device calculation when the timetable source is unreachable
Madinah mus-haf reading with recitation and word-by-word study modes
Prayer journal, fasting log and saved places stored encrypted on the device
Ad-free with no accounts and no Google Play Services in the F-Droid build
Also published for iOS, Mac, Windows, Linux and in the browser
entries.insight: Prayer-time apps usually argue about astronomy; Mihrab argues about trust. Matching an official printed timetable, then caching it for offline use, is what makes the app usable in a mosque or on a plane, and the privacy section names exactly which numbers ever leave the phone.

entries.name: Traffic Light
entries.summary: Traffic Light counts the mobile and Wi-Fi data your phone actually moves, entirely on the device, and presents it as a status-bar indicator plus home-screen widgets. It tracks data plans separately for each SIM, keeps historical usage for review, and documents its own battery cost in the project wiki rather than asking users to take it on faith.
features: Per-SIM mobile data and Wi-Fi tracking with data plan limits
Status-bar network indicator and home-screen usage widgets
Historical usage series and at-a-glance analytics on the phone
Optional Shizuku or root setup for multi-SIM tracking
Battery cost measured and published in the project wiki
entries.insight: GlassWire-style monitoring is a well-worn idea on desktop and almost absent on Android, where the OS hides per-app traffic. Traffic Light's interesting part is method: it publishes measured battery figures and an optional Shizuku path, which is a more useful engineering disclosure than most paid utilities offer.

entries.name: Flex
entries.summary: Flex is an offline-first training log for strength and cardio work. You build your own workout plans, record weights, reps and rest periods while you train, and read progress back through exercise history and graphs. Everything is written to the device, so the app is usable in a gym without signal, and the same Flutter codebase ships on Android, Windows and iOS.
features: Custom workout plans rather than preset programmes
Live logging of weights, reps, cardio sessions and rest timers
Exercise history and progress graphs stored on the device
Works without an internet connection
Distributed on Google Play, F-Droid and the Microsoft Store
entries.insight: Gym apps trend towards coaching subscriptions and cloud accounts. Flex keeps the boring part local, which is the part that matters in a basement gym with no signal: the log still opens, and your data has no server to be stranded on.

entries.name: Network Scanner
entries.summary: Network Scanner maps the devices on the local Wi-Fi and names them as well as it can. It combines a parallel ICMP sweep with TCP fallback, the ARP cache, mDNS, SSDP/UPnP and NetBIOS, then adds OUI vendor lookups and OS fingerprinting from open ports and banners. Nothing leaves the phone: there are no ads, no tracking and no root requirement, and deeper ARP reads are opt-in through Shizuku or root.
features: Parallel ping sweep with TCP fallback for hosts that ignore ICMP
mDNS, SSDP/UPnP and NetBIOS discovery for printers, TVs, Chromecasts and Windows shares
MAC vendor lookup with detection of randomised addresses
OS fingerprinting and device-type icons from open ports and banners
Full 65,535-port scan with banner grabbing, or a quick common-port pass
Works offline with no ads and no tracking
entries.insight: The hard part of a network scanner is not finding hosts, it identifying them. This one stacks five discovery protocols and admits what it cannot do, including the Android 10 limit on MAC addresses and the opt-in Shizuku route around it.

entries.name: Markleaf
entries.summary: Markleaf is a local-first Markdown note app that tries to make plain Markdown feel like an editor rather than a text box. A slash command inserts headings, tables, callouts and wikilinks as ordinary Markdown, footnotes jump between reference and definition, and tags are inferred from hashes in the body instead of a folder tree. The developer currently pauses Play updates pending a Korean business-registration requirement, so F-Droid and GitHub Releases carry the current build.
features: Quick-insert commands that write standard Markdown rather than rich text
GFM tables, checkboxes, blockquotes and callouts rendered in preview
Syntax highlighting for ten languages inside code blocks
Bidirectional footnote jumping and in-note find and replace
Tag autocomplete from hashes in the note body, with no folders required
Hardware keyboard shortcuts and a choice of bundled or user-supplied fonts
entries.insight: Most note apps lock your text into their schema. Markleaf keeps writing standard Markdown and lets you bring your own font file, which is the right trade for a local-first tool: the notes stay readable by whatever replaces the app.

entries.name: PGPony
entries.summary: PGPony is an OpenPGP client that keeps the whole trust model on the phone. It encrypts, decrypts, signs and verifies text and files, generates modern RFC 9580 (OpenPGP v6) Ed25519 and X25519 keys protected with Argon2id, and can hold private keys on a hardware security key over NFC or USB. The foss build has no Google dependencies, and release APKs carry published hashes so the signer can be checked with AppVerifier.
features: Encrypt, decrypt, sign and verify messages and files on device
RFC 9580 OpenPGP v6 key generation with Argon2id passphrase protection
Private keys held on YubiKey 5 NFC or Token2 hardware over NFC or USB
Read-only password-store support, including hardware-key entries
Key discovery through WKD and the keys.openpgp.org verifying keyserver
Biometric lock, secure-screen flag and a Google-free foss flavour
entries.insight: Phone PGP is usually a compromise, because the private key sits in app storage. PGPony's differentiator is the opposite posture: keys can stay on a hardware token, and the project publishes signing certificate hashes so you can verify the APK you just installed before trusting it with anything.
